Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=6 \\ y-3z &=-13 \\ -x-y-z &=-4\end{aligned}\right. \qquad M = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{array} \right]
$$



We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 4\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}-6} & -24\end{array}\right].
$$



This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 4\end{array}\right]
$$



Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

As we saw before for elementary $2\times 2$ matrices, each elementary $3\times 3$ matrix $E$ is invertible, and the corresponding inverse is always an elementary matrix of the same type as $E.$ To illustrate, let's consider the matrix 

$$
E = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To find the inverse of $E,$ we proceed as follows:

**Step 1:** Write down $\color{blue}E$ and the identity matrix $I_3$ side-by-side, as shown below:
$$
[{\color{blue}{E}}\, |\, {\color{black}I_3}]	
=	
\left[{\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}4} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0} & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}1} & 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}}\right]
$$

**Step 2:** Apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix. In our case, we need to apply the transformation $R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1.$ We apply the operation to entire row (not only the left part):

$$
\begin{aligned}[{\color{blue}E}\hspace{0.167em}|\hspace{0.167em}{\color{black}{I}_{3}}] & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}4} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0} & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}1} & 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 0 & 0 & {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & {\color{red}-4} & {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}0} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}1}\end{array}\right] \\  & =[{\color{black}{I}_{3}}\hspace{0.167em}|\hspace{0.167em}{\color{red}{E}^{-1}}]\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1$ transforms $E$ back into the identity matrix. Likewise, when this row operation is applied to the identity matrix, it generates $E^{-1}.$

The matrix $E^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,
$$
E^{-1} = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ - 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

We can work out the inverse of all elementary $3\times 3$ matrices in a similar way.

Remember the following three standard elementary row operations: 

  I. Swapping two rows

  II. Multiplying a row by a non-zero number

  III. Adding a multiple of one row to another row

Of these three elementary row operations, only III (adding a multiple of one row to another row) *preserves* the determinant. The other two operations, switching two rows or multiplying a row by a non-zero number, *change* the determinant.

To demonstrate, let's consider the matrix $A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{array} \right]}.$ Taking the determinant, we have
$$
\left| {\begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{array}} \right| = 1 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 3 = -2.
$$

If we swap the two rows, we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 4 \\  & =2 \\  & \ne -2\hspace{1em}{\color{red}\times }\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, if we multiply top row by ${\color{red}2},$ then we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}{\color{red}2}\cdot 1 & {\color{red}2}\cdot 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot 4-3\cdot 4 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne -2\hspace{1em}{\color{red}\times }\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we add twice the top row to the bottom row, then we get the same determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3+{\color{red}2}\cdot 1 & 4+{\color{red}2}\cdot 2\end{vmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot 8-2\cdot 5 \\  & =-2\hspace{1em}{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

A **basis** of a subspace $U$ (in $\mathbb{R}^n$) is a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is linearly independent and spans $U.$

For example, consider the following subspace consisting of the span of three vectors:
$$
U = \textrm{Span}
	\Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{blue}0}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{red}- 1} \\ {\color{red}3}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} 
	\Bigg\}
$$

To find a basis of $U,$ we need to find a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $U.$

**Watch out!** The set
$$
\Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{blue}0}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{red}- 1} \\ {\color{red}3}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} 
	\Bigg\}
$$
is *not* a basis of $U.$ It's true that this set *spans* $U,$ but the vectors in this set are *not* linearly independent. In particular, the vector $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2$ as follows:

$$
\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{red}- 1} \\ {\color{red}3}\end{array} \right]} }_{\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = 
	(-1) \cdot \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{blue}0}\end{array} \right]} }_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + 
	3 \cdot \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]} }_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}
$$

To find a basis of $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ we can start with $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ but we need to remove any "redundant" vectors that can be written as a linear combination of other vectors in the set. In this case, we remove ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}$ because it can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

We are left with the set

$$
\Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{blue}0}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}
	\Bigg\}.
$$

These two vectors are linearly independent (since they are not parallel), and removing a redundant vector does not change the span, so these vectors still span $U.$ That is to say,

$$
U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \} = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.
$$

Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B} = \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ is a basis of $U.$

**Note:** To see that the vectors $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ still span $U,$ first note that any vector $\mathbf{b} \in U$ can be written as a linear combination of the three original vectors:

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + x_2 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} + x_3 {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}
$$

Since ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = -{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}+3{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ then we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b} & ={x}_{1}{\color{blue}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{\color{blue}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}}+{x}_{3}(-{\color{blue}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}}+3{\color{blue}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}}) \\  & =({x}_{1}-{x}_{3}){\color{blue}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}}+({x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}){\color{blue}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{b}$ can actually be written as a linear combination of only two vectors, ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

Therefore, we can conclude that the set $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ spans the subspace $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \}.$

As we saw, swapping two rows does not preserve the determinant. However, the only difference is the sign of the determinant changes. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}{\color{red}1} & {\color{red}2} \\ {\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}4}\end{vmatrix} & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ \begin{vmatrix}{\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}4} \\ {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}2}\end{vmatrix} & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 4=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}{\color{red}1} & {\color{red}2} \\ {\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}4}\end{vmatrix} & =-\begin{vmatrix}{\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}4} \\ {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}2}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, swapping any two rows of a matrix changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one. That is to say, 

$$
\begin{aligned}det\begin{bmatrix}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ {\color{red}◻} & {\color{red}◻} & … & {\color{red}◻} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ {\color{blue}△} & {\color{blue}△} & … & {\color{blue}△} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{bmatrix}=-det\begin{bmatrix}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ {\color{blue}△} & {\color{blue}△} & … & {\color{blue}△} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ {\color{red}◻} & {\color{red}◻} & … & {\color{red}◻} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

As we have seen, multiplying a row by a number does not preserve the determinant. However, it does affect the determinant in a predictable way: multiplying a row by a number scales the determinant by that number as well.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ \begin{vmatrix}{\color{red}2}\cdot 1 & {\color{red}2}\cdot 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =2\cdot 4-3\cdot 4=-4\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have
$$
\left| {\begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}2} \cdot  1 & {\color{red}2} \cdot  2 \\ 3 & 4\end{array}} \right| = {\color{red}2} \cdot \left| {\begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{array}} \right|.
$$

In general, multiplying a row of a matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the row of the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det\begin{bmatrix}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ {\color{red}k}△ & {\color{red}k}△ & … & {\color{red}k}△ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{bmatrix}={\color{red}k}\cdot det\begin{bmatrix}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ △ & △ & … & △ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check what happens if we multiply the entire matrix (not only one row) by a number. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ \begin{vmatrix}{\color{red}3}\cdot 1 & {\color{red}3}\cdot 2 \\ {\color{red}3}\cdot 3 & {\color{red}3}\cdot 4\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 9 & 12\end{vmatrix} & =3\cdot 12-6\cdot 9=-18\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have

$$
\left| {\begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}3} \cdot  1 & {\color{red}3} \cdot  2 \\ {\color{red}3} \cdot  3 & {\color{red}3} \cdot  4\end{array}} \right| = {\color{red}3}^2 \cdot \left| {\begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{array}} \right|.
$$

The above is equivalent to multiplying both rows of the matrix by $3$. Multiplying the first row scales the determinant by $3$, and then multiplying the second row scales it by $3$ once more.

In general, multiplying an entire $n \times n$ matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number to the power of $n$. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the entire matrix, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A) &={k}^{n}\cdot det(A),\end{aligned}
$$

where $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix.

In the previous example, it was easy to see that one vector was a linear combination of the others. But what can we do when it's not so easy to tell? For example, consider the subspace

$$
U = \textrm{Span}
	\Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 7\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_3} 
	\Bigg\}.
$$

To find a subset of linearly independent vectors, we can put the vectors in a matrix and compute the reduced row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \phantom{=\hspace{0.222em}\hspace{0.167em}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{blue}1}} & 0 & {\color{red}4} \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{blue}1}} & {\color{red}5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent (or redundant) vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $2$nd columns are pivot columns, while the $3$rd column is a non-pivot column.

**But watch out!** We need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $2$nd columns from the original matrix are $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$ So, a basis of $U$ is $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ that is to say, 

$$
\mathcal{B} = \Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2} 
	\Bigg\}.
$$

We say that two vectors $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are **linearly independent** if the only solution to the equation

$$
x_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{0}
$$

is $x_1 = x_2 = 0.$ Otherwise, if there exists any solution other than $x_1 = x_2 = 0,$ then we say that the two vectors $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are **linearly dependent**.

To illustrate, let's consider two sets of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2\mathbin{:}$

$$
{\color{blue}
\textrm{I.}\:\: \Bigg\{ \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_1}, \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} \Bigg\}
}
{\color{red}
\qquad\qquad
\textrm{II.}\:\: \Bigg\{ \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{b}_1}, \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 2 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{b}_2} \Bigg\}
}
$$

- For the first set ${\color{blue}(\textrm{I})},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{\color{blue}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{\color{blue}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}} & =\mathbf{0} \\ {x}_{1}{\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}+{x}_{2}{\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}} & =\mathbf{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is true only if $x_1=x_2=0.$ So, the set $\color{blue}(\textrm{I})$ is *linearly independent*.

- On the other hand, for the second set ${\color{red}(\textrm{II})},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{\color{red}{\mathbf{b}}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{\color{red}{\mathbf{b}}_{2}} & =\mathbf{0} \\ {x}_{1}{\color{red}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}+{x}_{2}{\color{red}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}} & =\mathbf{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has solutions other than $x_1=x_2=0.$ For example, $x_1=2$ and $x_2=1$ gives
$$
2 \cdot {\color{red}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}} + 1 \cdot {\color{red}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 2 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}} = \mathbf{0}.
$$
Therefore, the set $\color{red}(\textrm{II})$ is *not* linearly independent. Rather, it is *linearly dependent*.

**Note:** You may notice that the vectors in the set $\color{red}(\textrm{II})$ were parallel (i.e. multiples of one another), while the vectors in set $\color{blue}(\textrm{I})$ were not. This trend holds in general, for all sets of two vectors:

- a set of two vectors is *linearly dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel, while

- a set of two vectors is *linearly independent* if and only if the two vectors are not parallel.

The set of vectors $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n \}$ in an abstract vector space $V$ is **linearly dependent** if there exist real scalars $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ not all zero such that 

$$
x_1\mathbf{v}_1+x_2\mathbf{v}_2+\ldots+x_n\mathbf{v}_n=\mathbf{0}.
$$

Otherwise, if $x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n = 0$ is the only solution, the set is **linearly independent**.

Let's consider some examples.

- First, let's consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}[t]$ of all polynomials in variable $t,$ along with the set

$$
S = \big\{ \underbrace{1}_{\color{blue}p_1(t)}, \: \underbrace{t}_{\color{blue}p_2(t)}, \: \underbrace{t^2}_{\color{blue}p_3(t)} \big\}.
$$

To determine whether $S$ is linearly dependent in $\mathbb{R}[t],$ we must solve the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{\color{blue}{p}_{1}(t)}+{x}_{2}{\color{blue}{p}_{2}(t)}+{x}_{3}{\color{blue}{p}_{3}(t)} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given expressions for $p_1(t),p_2(t)$ and $p_3(t)$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\cdot 1+{x}_{2}\cdot t+{x}_{3}\cdot {t}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}t+{x}_{3}{t}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=0 \\ {x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since $x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 0$ is the only solution, $S$ is linearly independent in $\mathbb R[t].$

- Let's consider the vector space $\mathbb R[t]$ once more, along with the set 

$$
T = \big\{ \underbrace{t^2+1}_{\color{red}q_1(t)}, \: \underbrace{-2t^2-2}_{\color{red}q_2(t)} \big\}.
$$

To determine whether $T$ is linearly dependent in $\mathbb{R}[t],$ we must solve the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{\color{red}{q}_{1}(t)}+{x}_{2}{\color{red}{q}_{2}(t)} & =0 \\ {x}_{1}({t}^{2}+1)+{x}_{2}(-2{t}^{2}-2) & =0 \\ ({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})+({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}){t}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This system has the nonzero solution $(x_1,x_2)=(2,1).$ As a result, we get

$$
2 \cdot {\color{red}q_1(t)} + 1 \cdot {\color{red}q_2(t)} = 0.
$$

Therefore, the set $\big\{ q_1(t), q_2(t) \big\}$ is linearly dependent in $\mathbb R[t].$

If an $n\!\times \!n$ matrix $A$ has an entire row or column of zeros, then its determinant is equal to zero.

For example, consider the matrix $A$ given below:

$$
A=
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\end{array} \right]}
$$

The second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ($\ast$) may represent any number.

Let's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)^{2+1}({\color{red}0})\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix}+(-1)^{2+2}({\color{red}0})\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix}+(-1)^{2+3}({\color{red}0})\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0+0+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ($\ast$). Each cofactor is multiplied by zero, so the final result must be zero.

Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows but it has two identical rows:

$$
A  = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

We can subtract the $1$st row from the $3$rd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1}\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Since this operation does not change the determinant, we get $\det(A) = \det(B).$ Furthermore, as $B$ contains a zero row, we obtain

$$
\det(A) = \det(B) = 0.
$$

Notice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:

*If a square matrix has at least two identical rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.*

Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows and no identical rows but it has two proportional rows:

$$
A  = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{blue}- 3} & {\color{blue}- 6} & {\color{blue}- 3}\end{array} \right]}
$$

We can add three times the $1$st row to the $3$rd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{blue}-3} & {\color{blue}-6} & {\color{blue}-3}\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Since this operation does not change the determinant, we get $\det(A) = \det(B).$ Furthermore, as $B$ contains a zero row, we obtain

$$
\det(A) = \det(B) = 0.
$$

Notice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:

*If a square matrix has at least two proportional rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.*

$$

If ${x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=\mathbf{b}$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-7 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{1} \\ -3{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-7{x}_{2} \\ 5{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{1}-7{x}_{2} \\ -3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-7{x}_{2} &=-9 \\ -3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=3 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Adding the first and the second equations we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} & =-6 \\ {x}_{2} & =3,\end{aligned}

which we substitute into the second equation to get 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1 \\ (4)-(3) & =1 \\ 1 & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=4$ and ${x}_{2}=3,$ which means

$$

$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=4+3=7.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

$$

Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 3 \\ -5 & -10 & -15 \end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=3\\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x+2y=3.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=3-2y,$ and the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=3-2y\\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
